title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
seo_title: Year 11 Science: Photosynthesis and Respiration Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: Photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction and its equation; the rate of photosynthesis and limiting factors (temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide); the inverse square law (higher tier); uses of glucose; aerobic and anaerobic respiration; the response to exercise and the oxygen debt; metabolism.
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on bioenergetics: photosynthesis, limiting factors, the inverse square law, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, exercise and oxygen debt. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it.
key_sub: Anaerobic respiration in muscles makes lactic acid only.
body_html:
How to think about it

Plants make glucose; every living cell respires it.

  • Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy is taken in).
  • The rate is limited by light, carbon dioxide or temperature. Light intensity ∝ 1/distance².
  • Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Anaerobic in muscles: glucose → lactic acid. In yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
Example

Lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm. Light intensity?

2 × distance

1/2² = 1/4

Answer: 1/4 as much

Example

Products of anaerobic respiration in muscles?

No oxygen used

Answer: lactic acid

Common mistakes

  • Thinking plants get their glucose from the soil.
  • Thinking anaerobic respiration in muscles makes carbon dioxide.
  • Thinking double the distance gives half the light (it is a quarter).

faq.q: What limits the rate of photosynthesis?
faq.a: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. The one in shortest supply is the limiting factor.

faq.q: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
faq.a: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases much more energy. Anaerobic respiration does not use oxygen; in muscles it makes lactic acid, in yeast it makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with the lactic acid that built up in the muscles.
